title: Spring Lecture #16: DTOs & Validations in Spring Boot

questions.question: For a `String name` field, which single annotation rejects all three of these values: `null`, `""` and `"   "`?
options: `@NotNull`
`@NotBlank`
`@NotEmpty`
`@Size(min = 1)`
questions.explanation: `@NotBlank` rejects null, empty and whitespace-only strings, which is why the lecture prefers it for names and emails. `@NotNull` accepts `""`, and `@NotEmpty` rejects null and `""` but accepts `"   "` because spaces give it a non-zero length.

questions.question: The controller accepts the `Student` entity directly with `@RequestBody Student student`. The entity has fields like `role`, `isVerified` and `isDeleted`. What is the main risk the lecture describes?
options: The client can send internal fields such as `"role":"ADMIN"` or `"isDeleted":false`, and the backend accidentally accepts them (mass assignment)
Entities cannot be converted from JSON, so the request always fails
JPA refuses to save an entity that was created by Jackson
The entity makes the request slower because Hibernate validates every field
questions.explanation: When the entity is the request model, the outside world can set any of its fields, including ones only the backend should control (id, flags, role, timestamps); the notes call this the mass assignment problem. Jackson can map JSON into an entity without trouble, which is exactly why the danger exists.

questions.question: A teammate added `@NotBlank`, `@Email` and `@Min(18)` to `CreateStudentRequestDto`, but the controller method is `createStudent(@RequestBody CreateStudentRequestDto dto)`. Students with blank names and age 5 are still being saved. What is missing?
options: The annotations must be moved to the `Student` entity to take effect
`@RequestBody` must be replaced with `@ModelAttribute` for validation to run
The service must call `dto.validate()` before mapping
`@Valid` on the parameter: the annotations only define the rules, and `@Valid` tells Spring to apply them
questions.explanation: The notes separate the two parts: constraint annotations define the rules, and `@Valid @RequestBody` triggers validation after JSON is converted. Without `@Valid`, the DTO reaches the service unchecked. Moving rules to the entity is the wrong direction; request rules belong on the request DTO.

questions.question: The client posts the body below to `POST /api/students`, whose parameter is `@Valid @RequestBody CreateStudentRequestDto`. What happens?
options: 400, reporting only the name error, because validation stops at the first failure
201 Created, because every field is present and non-null
400 with errors for `name`, `age` and `email`; the service method is never called
400 with errors for `name`, `age`, `email` and `rollNo`
questions.explanation: All constraints are checked: "A" is not blank but violates `@Size(min = 2)`, 17 violates `@Min(18)`, and "abc" is not a valid email; `rollNo` (5) and `subject` pass. Validation failure means 400 Bad Request and the service is not invoked. Bean Validation collects all violations rather than stopping at the first one.

questions.question: A client tries to cheat by posting extra fields to the lecture's create API (Spring Boot 4 defaults). Assuming all validations pass and the email is new, what does the response contain?
options: 201 with `"id": 100` and `"deleted": true`, because the client supplied them
400, because the body contains fields the DTO does not declare
201 with `"id": 100`, but `deleted` is reset to false
201 with a database-generated id, the success message and timestamps, and no `deleted` field at all
questions.explanation: `id` and `deleted` have no place in the request DTO, so they are ignored during JSON conversion (unknown properties do not fail by default here), and the service sets `deleted=false` and lets MySQL generate the id. The response DTO has no `deleted` field, so it never leaks. This is exactly how the request DTO protects the API boundary.
questions.source: code: StudentService.java, CreateStudentRequestDto.java, CreateStudentResponseDto.java; notes p13-p20

questions.question: The lecture's `UpdateStudentRequestDto` has `name`, `age`, `rollNo` and `subject`, but no `email`. A client calls the update API and includes `"email":"new@x.com"` in the body. What happens to the student's email?
options: It is updated, because the entity has an `email` field
It stays unchanged: the update DTO has no email field, so the value is never read, which is how the API forbids email changes
The request fails with 400 because `email` is not allowed
It is set to null, because the DTO's missing email overwrites the old one
questions.explanation: The notes use exactly this example: create may allow email while update does not, so each API defines its own contract. The extra JSON property is ignored, and the service never calls `setEmail` during update, so the stored email stays as it was. Nothing in the update DTO could set it to null either.

questions.question: For database reasons, the `Student` entity's `name` is split into `firstName` and `lastName`. The mobile app still expects `"name": "Amit Sharma"` in responses. How do response DTOs help?
options: The response DTO keeps a `name` field and the service maps `firstName + " " + lastName` into it, so the API contract does not change
The response DTO automatically mirrors the entity, so the app sees the new fields with no code change
DTOs force the database column to stay named `name`
They do not help; the mobile app must be updated whenever the entity changes
questions.explanation: Because the API returns a separate response DTO filled by explicit mapping, internal changes stay internal: only the mapping code changes. If the entity were returned directly, the JSON would switch to `firstName`/`lastName` and break the client, which is the lecture's Problem 5. DTOs do not mirror entities automatically; mapping is written by hand in the service.

questions.question: Why does the lecture put request validations (`@NotBlank`, `@Email`, `@Min`) on the request DTOs instead of on the `Student` entity?
options: Because Bean Validation annotations cannot compile on classes annotated with `@Entity`
Because putting them on the DTO makes the database enforce them as column constraints
Because the rules describe what a client may send to a specific API, and different APIs (create vs update) need different rules, while the entity is one shared internal model
Because `@Valid` only works on classes whose names end with `Dto`
questions.explanation: Validation is about the request contract: create requires email, update does not even accept it, so each request DTO carries its own rules and `@Valid` checks them before the service runs. The entity is shared by all operations and represents the table. Bean Validation can technically annotate entities, so it is a design choice, not a compiler limit.

questions.question: A teammate deletes `@NotNull` from `age` but keeps `@Min(18)`. A client posts a valid body that simply omits `age`. The entity's field is `private int age` with `setAge(int age)`. What happens?
options: 400, because `@Min(18)` rejects a missing value
Validation passes (`@Min` treats null as valid), then `setAge(dto.getAge())` unboxes null and throws `NullPointerException`, so the request ends in a 500
The student is saved with age 0, the default for `int`
The student is saved with age 18, the minimum allowed
questions.explanation: Bean Validation constraints like `@Min` and `@Size` consider null valid, so only `@NotNull` would catch a missing age. The null `Integer` then reaches `setAge(int)`, where auto-unboxing throws `NullPointerException`, a server error rather than a clean 400. That is why the lecture pairs `@NotNull` with `@Min`.
questions.source: code: CreateStudentRequestDto.java, StudentService.java, Student.java; notes p27-p30

questions.question: `name` has both `@NotBlank(message = "Name cannot be null/Empty or blank")` and `@Size(min = 2, max = 50, ...)`. A client sends a body with no `name` property at all (other fields valid). Which validation error(s) are reported for `name`?
options: Only "Name cannot be null/Empty or blank", because `@Size` treats null as valid
Both messages, because a missing name is shorter than 2 characters
Only the `@Size` message, because it is declared last
No error, because missing properties are skipped by validation
questions.explanation: A missing property leaves the field null. `@NotBlank` rejects null, but `@Size` only checks the length of a non-null value, so it passes. This is why `@Size` alone would not make a field required. Validation is not skipped for missing properties: the DTO field is simply null and every constraint is evaluated against that value.
